input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-250: Concepts of Computer Systems. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: An introduction to the hardware and software organization of computer systems. The course emphasizes a multilevel model of computer organization. Topics include the digital logic level; the micro architecture level; the machine instruction set level; the operating system level; and the assembly language level. Programming assignments will be required. Prerequisites: (CSCI-243 or 4003-334) and (MATH-190 or MATH-200 or 1016-366) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

Source excerpts:

[mit-xv6-book]
The xv6 book explains processes, system calls, traps, page tables, scheduling, locking, file systems, devices, concurrency, and isolation in a small Unix-like kernel. A process combines an address space with execution state and operating-system resources. A system call transfers control from user code to a privileged kernel service. A trap records processor state so the kernel can handle a system call, exception, or interrupt. Page tables map virtual addresses to physical memory with permission bits. The scheduler selects runnable processes and switches processor context. Locks protect invariants when concurrent execution can access shared state. The file system organizes persistent data through inodes, directories, and logged updates. Analysis distinguishes user mode, privileged kernel code, hardware translation, interrupt state, resource ownership, and synchronization invariants.

[riscv-unprivileged]
The RISC-V ISA defines programmer-visible instructions, registers, memory operations, control transfer, exceptions, and ordering behavior. Integer register x0 always reads as zero, while the remaining integer registers hold software-visible values. Load instructions transfer data from memory into registers. Store instructions transfer register data to memory. Branch and jump instructions change control flow. Exceptions report conditions that require a defined transfer of control. Memory-ordering rules constrain how memory operations may be observed. Architecture analysis preserves data dependencies, control dependencies, and architectural state.

[rit-csci-250]
An introduction to the hardware and software organization of computer systems. The course emphasizes a multilevel model of computer organization. Topics include the digital logic level; the micro architecture level; the machine instruction set level; the operating system level; and the assembly language level. Programming assignments will be required. Prerequisites: (CSCI-243 or 4003-334) and (MATH-190 or MATH-200 or 1016-366) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

beats.claim: Computer systems are organized into a multilevel model that spans from digital logic to high-level operating systems.
beats.example: This hierarchy allows developers to write assembly code that directly manipulates registers while the OS handles memory and scheduling.
beats.title: Introduction to Multilevel Architecture
beats.visualDirection: Display a stacked diagram showing five layers: digital logic, microarchitecture, instruction set, OS, and assembly, with arrows indicating upward abstraction and downward control.

beats.claim: The digital logic level implements basic gates and circuits that form the foundation for all subsequent hardware components.
beats.example: A simple AND gate combines two input signals to produce a single output, enabling complex logic in modern processors.
beats.title: Digital Logic and Microarchitecture Basics
beats.visualDirection: Show a schematic of basic logic gates (AND, OR, NOT) connected to form a simple adder, highlighting signal flow.

beats.claim: Microarchitecture translates high-level instructions into precise hardware operations that execute on the processor.
beats.example: A branch instruction alters the control flow by updating the program counter based on a condition evaluated by the CPU.
beats.title: Microarchitecture and Instruction Set Interface
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a pipeline diagram showing how an instruction moves through fetch, decode, execute, and write-back stages.

beats.claim: The machine instruction set defines the precise commands that programmers can issue to control hardware behavior.
beats.example: A load instruction transfers data from a memory address into a specific register for subsequent computation.
beats.title: Machine Instruction Set Level
beats.visualDirection: Display a table mapping common RISC-V instructions to their register and memory operands, emphasizing data flow.

beats.claim: The operating system manages hardware resources and provides an interface for multiple programs to run concurrently.
beats.example: The OS allocates CPU time to different processes using a scheduler that prioritizes runnable tasks.
beats.title: Operating System Level Overview
beats.visualDirection: Draw a flowchart showing process creation, scheduling decision, context switch, and resource allocation steps.

beats.claim: Processes execute in user mode for normal tasks, while privileged operations require a transition to kernel mode.
beats.example: A system call transfers control from user code to a privileged kernel service to access hardware or manage memory.
beats.title: User Mode and Kernel Mode Transitions
beats.visualDirection: Show a side-by-side comparison of user mode (restricted permissions) and kernel mode (full hardware access) with a transition arrow.

beats.claim: System calls use traps to safely transfer control to the kernel while preserving processor state for later return.
beats.example: When a process requests file I/O, a trap records the CPU registers so the kernel can handle the request and restore state.
beats.title: System Calls and Traps Mechanism
beats.visualDirection: Create a sequence diagram showing the trap entry, kernel handling, and return path with state preservation markers.

beats.claim: Page tables map virtual addresses to physical memory locations, enabling efficient memory management and protection.
beats.example: A page table entry contains a physical address pointer and permission bits that determine access rights for each memory block.
beats.title: Virtual Memory and Page Tables
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a two-level page table structure with arrows linking virtual addresses to physical frames, highlighting permission bits.

beats.claim: Locks protect shared resources from concurrent access, while the scheduler ensures fair CPU distribution among processes.
beats.example: A mutex lock prevents two processes from modifying a shared counter simultaneously, maintaining data integrity.
beats.title: Concurrency, Locks, and Scheduling
beats.visualDirection: Display a diagram of a shared resource with a lock mechanism, showing how processes queue and acquire exclusive access.

beats.claim: Students can verify system behavior by checking data dependencies, control flow, and resource ownership across all levels.
beats.example: An analyst reviews a process trace to confirm that traps preserved state, locks protected invariants, and page tables mapped correctly.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Provide a checklist template with boxes for verifying: state preservation, lock invariants, page table mappings, and scheduling fairness.

learningObjectives: Define the multilevel model of computer organization and explain how each level interfaces with the levels above and below it.
Explain the role of system calls, traps, and user/kernel mode transitions in managing privileged operations and resource access.
Apply the concepts of virtual memory, scheduling, and concurrency to analyze how operating systems manage multiple processes efficiently.
